The distinction from cultural competence framed as mastery of a finite body of knowledge, and why the authors proposed humility as the better training outcome

The practitioner as learner about this person's life rather than expert on their group; asking rather than assuming, checking one's interpretation, noticing when one's own norms are doing the judging, and repairing after getting it wrong

claims.claim: Cultural humility was proposed by Melanie Tervalon and Jann Murray-Garcia in an article published in the Journal of Health Care for the Poor and Underserved in May 1998, volume 9, issue 2, pages 117-125, addressed to the problem of defining and evaluating training outcomes in multicultural medical education.

Tervalon and Murray-Garcia defined cultural humility as three sustained commitments: a lifelong commitment to self-evaluation and self-critique, a commitment to redressing the power imbalances in the patient-physician dynamic, and a commitment to developing mutually beneficial and non-paternalistic clinical and advocacy partnerships with communities on behalf of individuals and defined populations.

Their objection was to competence as it is traditionally construed in clinical training - an easily demonstrable mastery of a finite body of knowledge, evidenced largely by comparative quantitative assessments - which they argued is the wrong model for this area of physician education because it sets a discrete endpoint where there is none.

The 1998 article explicitly states that the authors are in no way discounting the value of knowing as much as possible about the health care practices of the communities served, and it offers the example of a Cambodian child presenting with the marks of coining, a Southeast Asian healing practice, which should not be mistaken for evidence of child abuse; the authors argue that knowledge must run simultaneously with realistic and ongoing self-appraisal.

The article illustrates the failure mode of competence-as-mastery with a case in which a nurse who had taken a cross-cultural course dismissed a colleague's observation that a post-surgical patient appeared to be in a great deal of pain, on the basis of what she believed she knew about how patients of that background express pain; the authors describe this as stereotyping the patient's experience and ignoring clues to her present reality.

The authors describe humility as a prerequisite for a process in which the practitioner relinquishes the role of expert to the patient and becomes the student of the patient, supported by a less controlling, less authoritative interviewing style that signals that the practitioner values the patient's own agenda and perspectives; they argue this removes the need for complete mastery of every group's health beliefs, because the patient is the one who conveys how much culture has to do with a particular encounter.

The term intersectionality is attributed to Kimberle Crenshaw, who introduced it in Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex, published in the University of Chicago Legal Forum, Volume 1989, Article 8; in health and human-service scholarship it refers to social positions such as race, class, gender, disability and sexuality intersecting to shape each other within structures of power, so that experiences of marginalisation cannot be analysed one category at a time and no group is internally homogeneous.

Lekas, Pahl and Fuller Lewis argue that training practitioners to be competent in particular cultures risks stereotyping, stigmatising and othering the people they serve, because a static and totalising account of a group's beliefs functions as a social stereotype, and that intersectionality further undermines single-group training because treating race or sexual orientation as a master status risks essentialising the individual; this is their argued position, published in a peer-reviewed journal, not a settled empirical finding.

Reviewing roughly two decades of published evaluations, Lekas and colleagues report that cultural competence trainings vary widely in scope, length, content and delivery, that they primarily increase practitioner knowledge, attitudes and self-efficacy, and that they have shown little or no demonstrated effect on patient satisfaction or on health outcomes that would reduce disparities.

Lekas and colleagues go further and recommend abandoning the term cultural competence altogether; other scholarship treats cultural humility and cultural safety as critiques of, and in some accounts as foundations for, cultural competence rather than as a replacement, and the two vocabularies are frequently used together in practice literature. The disagreement is live and the lesson attributes rather than resolves it.

Hook and colleagues (2013) defined cultural humility as an other-oriented rather than self-focused interpersonal stance marked by respect and a lack of superiority toward a person's cultural background, developed a client-rated measure of a therapist's cultural humility across four studies, and found that clients' perceptions of their therapist's cultural humility were positively associated with a strong working alliance and with improvement in therapy, with the alliance mediating that association.

The outcome evidence for cultural humility is young, largely correlational and dependent on self-report and client-report instruments; reviews report discrepancies in how the concept is defined across the literature, note that cultural competence itself lacks agreed definitions, observe that much of the cultural humility work remains theoretical, and call for clearer conceptualisation, better measurement and the inclusion of service-recipient voices in evaluating effectiveness.

The National CLAS Standards, issued by the Office of Minority Health at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, are fifteen action steps: a Principal Standard requiring effective, understandable and respectful quality care and services that respond to cultural health beliefs and practices, languages, health literacy and other communication needs, plus standards grouped under Governance, Leadership and Workforce; Communication and Language Assistance; and Engagement, Continuous Improvement and Accountability.

CLAS Standard 5 calls for language assistance to be offered at no cost to the individual, Standard 6 for informing individuals of its availability, Standard 7 for ensuring the competence of those providing language assistance through training and certification where available while recognising that the use of untrained individuals and minors as interpreters should be avoided and discouraged, and Standards 12 and 13 for assessing community needs and partnering with the community to design, implement and evaluate services.

The National Council on Interpreting in Health Care publishes thirty-two standards of practice under nine headings; among them, interpreters render everything that is said and tell the parties so, promote direct communication by asking the parties to address each other rather than the interpreter, and limit their professional activity to interpreting, redirecting rather than advising.

Karliner and colleagues' systematic review of 28 studies found that across communication errors and comprehension, service utilisation, clinical outcomes and satisfaction, the use of professional interpreters was associated with better clinical care than the use of ad hoc interpreters, and appeared to bring quality for patients with limited English proficiency toward that of patients without a language barrier; this is an association reported in observational studies, not a controlled demonstration of cause.

The 2021 revision of the NASW Code of Ethics names cultural humility explicitly within ethical standard 1.05 on cultural competence, tying it to critical self-reflection, recognising clients as experts on their own culture, a commitment to continuous learning, and holding institutions accountable; the same standard also requires knowledge that supports culturally informed practice and education about social diversity and oppression. Codes differ by profession and jurisdiction, and licensure law governs practice.

Tervalon and Murray-Garcia extended the same demand for self-reflection and self-critique to institutions, asking what the demographic profile of the faculty is, what institutional processes contradict what is taught, and - as a concrete example - whether an institution that teaches practitioners not to use children or family members as translators actually provides an accessible alternative; they also called for time-limited, explicit goals to which communities could hold institutions publicly accountable.

Supervision in public human services is described by federal practice guidance as carrying administrative, educational and supportive functions and as promoting strengths-based, culturally responsive and trauma-informed approaches, which supports treating reflective practice as an organisational structure rather than an individual disposition.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether cultural humility should replace cultural competence or work alongside it
positions: Lekas, Pahl and Fuller Lewis (2020) argue for abandoning the term competence outright, on the grounds that claiming competence in a culture is untrue, invites stereotyping, and inflates the practitioner's authority.

Other conceptual literature surveyed by Konidaris and Petrakis (2025) treats cultural humility and cultural safety as critiques of, and in some accounts foundations for, cultural competence, with the vocabularies used together rather than as alternatives.

Tervalon and Murray-Garcia themselves did not reject knowledge or competence wholesale; they redefined the outcome, writing that cultural competence in clinical practice is best defined not by a discrete endpoint but as commitment and active engagement in a lifelong process.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the distinction as the heart of the topic, names Lekas and colleagues' stronger claim as their position rather than as consensus, and states that in current practice literature the two vocabularies frequently appear together. It takes no side.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How strong the outcome evidence for cultural humility is
positions: Hook and colleagues (2013) report positive associations between client-perceived therapist cultural humility, working alliance and improvement in therapy.

Lekas and colleagues note that most cultural humility work remains theoretical and call for clearer conceptualisation and measurement; Konidaris and Petrakis report discrepancies in concept definitions across the literature and did not assess source quality.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states that the concept is measured mainly by self-report and client-report instruments, that the outcome literature is young and largely correlational, and that reviews report definitional inconsistency. It does not assert that cultural humility has been shown to improve outcomes.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the evidence on interpreters supports a causal claim
positions: Karliner and colleagues (2007) found professional interpreter use associated with better care than ad hoc interpreter use across all four areas examined.
The included studies are observational comparisons, not randomised trials, and the review is now nearly two decades old.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the association and the direction of the finding, and says explicitly that it is an association from observational studies. The binding practice point rests on CLAS Standard 7, which is a standard rather than an empirical claim.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft asserted that cultural humility is 'a foundational concept in Social Work & Human Services' and described it only as a term students use to organise information. Nothing in the draft identified Tervalon and Murray-Garcia, the 1998 article, the three commitments, the contrast with cultural competence, power, intersectionality, CLAS, or the state of the evidence.
The draft's Eli-10 analogy ('a label on a toolbox drawer', 'reading a map legend') carried no content about the concept and was discarded.
The draft's vocabulary entries ('context', 'evidence', 'application') were generic study-skills terms with no relation to this topic.
The draft's question bank tested only generic study behaviour ('memorising the term without context'), had three options per item, and did not test the topic at all.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire draft with content anchored in the 1998 primary article, read page by page from a scanned copy of the published text.
Added the three commitments in the authors' own terms, attributed and dated.
Added the competence contrast, including the authors' explicit refusal to discount knowledge about communities, so that the lesson cannot be read as endorsing ignorance.
Added intersectionality with attribution to Crenshaw and a substantive characterisation carried by sources that were actually readable.
Added the CLAS standards and interpreter practice as the structural and concrete anchors the draft lacked.
Replaced unqualified effectiveness language with an explicit statement of what the measurement and outcome literature can and cannot show.
Added an explicit educational-material statement and removed anything that could read as individualised clinical or cultural advice.

sourceRecords.title: Cultural Humility Versus Cultural Competence: A Critical Distinction in Defining Physician Training Outcomes in Multicultural Education (Journal of Health Care for the Poor and Underserved, 9(2), 117-125)
sourceRecords.provider: Melanie Tervalon and Jann Murray-Garcia; Johns Hopkins University Press. Full text read from the scanned copy of the published article posted by the first author on her professional site; bibliographic record and abstract independently confirmed against the MEDLINE record served by Europe PMC (PMID 10073197, DOI 10.1353/hpu.2010.0233).
sourceRecords.notes: The originating source for the concept. Read page by page (pp. 117-125). Supports: the three commitments as the authors stated them; the objection to competence understood as an easily demonstrable mastery of a finite body of knowledge evidenced by comparative quantitative assessment; the nurse anecdote in which self-proclaimed cultural expertise led to a patient's postoperative pain being dismissed; the authors' explicit statement that they are in no way discounting the value of knowing as much as possible about the health care practices of the communities served; the coining example; the physician relinquishing the role of expert and becoming the student of the patient; patient-focused interviewing described as a less controlling, less authoritative style; Ridley's example of a patient's conjoint membership in eight cultural roles and the intersection of race, ethnicity, religion and class; the Institutional consistency section, including the question of whether an institution that teaches against using children or family members as translators actually provides an accessible alternative; and the authors' own statement that measurement of cultural competence was not a well-developed area of research. No wording is reproduced; all prose in the lesson is original.

sourceRecords.notes: Used here only for ethical standard 1.05 (Cultural Competence) in the 2021 revision, which names cultural humility explicitly in subsection (c) and ties it to critical self-reflection, recognising clients as experts on their own culture, a commitment to continuous learning, and holding institutions accountable; and for the surrounding subsections requiring knowledge for culturally informed practice and education about social diversity and oppression. sourceRecords.title: National Standards of Practice for Interpreters in Health Care
sourceRecords.provider: National Council on Interpreting in Health Care
sourceRecords.notes: September 2005; text extracted locally from the accessible PDF. Thirty-two standards under nine headings (Accuracy, Confidentiality, Impartiality, Respect, Cultural Awareness, Role Boundaries, Professionalism, Professional Development, Advocacy). Supports: interpreters render everything said and advise parties that everything will be interpreted (standards 1-6); the Respect standards, including standard 12, under which the interpreter promotes direct communication and may tell the patient and provider to address each other rather than the interpreter; standard 13 on promoting patient autonomy; the Cultural Awareness standards 14-15; and the Role Boundaries standards 16-18, under which the interpreter limits professional activity to interpreting and redirects rather than advises.

sourceRecords.title: Do Professional Interpreters Improve Clinical Care for Patients with Limited English Proficiency? A Systematic Review of the Literature (Health Services Research, 42(2), 727-754)
sourceRecords.provider: Leah S. Karliner, Elizabeth A. Jacobs, Alice Hm Chen and Sunita Mutha; Health Research and Educational Trust / Wiley. Record and full abstract read via the Europe PMC REST API (PMID 17362215, PMC1955368).
sourceRecords.notes: Systematic review of 28 included articles, 21 of which assessed professional interpreters separately from ad hoc interpreters. Supports the claim that across the four areas examined (communication errors and comprehension, utilisation, clinical outcomes, and satisfaction) use of professional interpreters was associated with better clinical care than use of ad hoc interpreters, and appeared to raise quality for patients with limited English proficiency toward that of patients without a language barrier. Cited for the direction of that association only; the review is observational evidence and the lesson does not present it as causal proof. Only the abstract was available; no full text was read and no wording is reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Rethinking Cultural Competence: Shifting to Cultural Humility (Health Services Insights, 13, 1178632920970580)
sourceRecords.provider: Helen-Maria Lekas, Kerstin Pahl and Crystal Fuller Lewis; SAGE Publications. Full text read via the Europe PMC REST API (PMC7756036).
sourceRecords.license: CC BY-NC 4.0 as stated in the article
sourceRecords.notes: A position paper, cited as an attributed argument rather than as settled fact. Supports: the authors' argument that training providers to become competent in various cultures risks stereotyping, stigmatising and othering; that a static and totalising view of culture generates a social stereotype; that intersectionality undermines single-group trainings because assuming race or sexual orientation is a master status risks essentialising the person; their reading of two decades of reviews, in which cultural competence training mainly increased provider knowledge, attitudes and self-efficacy with little or no demonstrated effect on patient satisfaction or health outcomes; their observation that raising provider self-assessed competence can intensify the power imbalance; their characterisation of humility training as process-oriented and competence training as content-oriented; their statement that most cultural humility work to date is theoretical; and their call for clearer conceptualisation and measurement. The lesson also names their stronger recommendation - abandoning the term competence - as their position, not as consensus. Licence permits non-commercial reuse only, so no wording is reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Cultural Humility Training in Mental Health Service Provision: A Scoping Review of the Foundational and Conceptual Literature (Healthcare, 13(11), 1342)
sourceRecords.provider: Mayio Konidaris (Victoria University) and Melissa Petrakis (Monash University); MDPI. Full text read via the Europe PMC REST API (PMC12155312).
sourceRecords.license: CC BY 4.0 as stated in the article
sourceRecords.notes: Scoping review of conceptual and training literature; 246 records extracted, 56 full texts reviewed. Supports: the statement that the review did not assess the depth or quality of sources and that concept definitions are discrepant across the literature; that cultural competence itself is described in the literature as lacking agreed mutual definitions; that cultural humility and cultural safety function as critiques of, and in some accounts as foundations for, cultural competence rather than as a wholly separate track; that cultural humility is not the most commonly adopted construct internationally and that terminology is inconsistent; and the recommendation that future research examine the effectiveness of such frameworks with service-recipient voices included. Original wording used; no text reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Cultural Humility: Measuring Openness to Culturally Diverse Clients (Journal of Counseling Psychology, 60(3), 353-366)
sourceRecords.provider: Joshua N. Hook, Don E. Davis, Jesse Owen, Everett L. Worthington Jr. and Shawn O. Utsey; American Psychological Association. Bibliographic record and abstract read via the Europe PMC REST API (PMID 23647387).
sourceRecords.notes: Supports: the definition of cultural humility as an other-oriented rather than self-focused interpersonal stance characterised by respect and a lack of superiority toward a person's cultural background and experience; the development across four studies of a client-rated measure of a therapist's cultural humility; and the finding that clients' perceptions of their therapist's cultural humility were positively associated with a strong working alliance and with improvement in therapy, with the alliance mediating that relationship.
